summary: Specifies new Name Type values for the ICMPv6 Trust Anchor option in SEcure Neighbor Discovery, based on certificate Subject Key Identifiers. It updates RFC 3971.

plainLanguage.summary: SEND needs a way to say which trusted authority it means. This adds a new way of naming, using the fingerprint of the authority's key.

questions: what is the send trust anchor option
what is a subject key identifier
what are send name type values
subtitle: New SEND Trust Anchor name types that identify a trust anchor by a hash of its Subject Key Identifier.

tldr.problem: The SEND Trust Anchor option could name an anchor only by X.501 name or FQDN, but certificate subject names are unique only within one CA and the RFC 6494 profile makes the Subject field meaningless.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6495 defines Name Type values 3 to 7 that carry a SHA-1, SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384 or SHA-512 hash of the certificate's Subject Key Identifier, and reserves or marks other values.
tldr.outcome: Routers can identify trust anchors across CAs. It also updates RFC 3971 by loosening the registration procedure for the Name Type registry.

today: RFC 6495 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3971. No later RFC obsoletes it.

sections.title: Why New Name Types
sections.content:
SEcure Neighbor Discovery (SEND, RFC 3971) uses X.509v3 certificates with the RFC 3779 extension to certify a router's authority over an IPv6 prefix. The Trust Anchor (TA) option lets a host identify the trust anchor it selected, and RFC 3971 defined two name types: a DER Encoded X.501 Name and a Fully Qualified Domain Name.

A certificate subject name is only unique within each Certification Authority, so a way to identify TAs across CAs is needed. In the certificate profile adopted for SEND by RFC 6494 and RFC 6487, the Subject field is declared meaningless and subjectAltName is not allowed, but the Subject Key Identifier (SKI) extension is mandatory and non-critical.
sections.plainLanguage: Two different authorities can have the same name, so names are not enough. A key fingerprint is different for each one.

sections.title: The New Name Type Values
sections.content:
The Name Type field in the ICMPv6 TA option gets these values: 3 SHA-1 SKI, 4 SHA-224 SKI, 5 SHA-256 SKI, 6 SHA-384 SKI and 7 SHA-512 SKI. Values 0 and 255 are reserved and not available for allocation, and 253-254 are experimental per RFC 3692.

Type 3 carries a 160-bit SHA-1 hash of the DER-encoded ASN.1 bit string of the subject public key, as described in Section 4.8.2 of RFC 6487. Types 4 to 7 use SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512 respectively. Implementations MAY support these name types.
sections.plainLanguage: Each number says which fingerprint recipe was used. A few numbers are kept back for testing or for later.

sections.title: Router Processing Rules
sections.content:
If the TA option is represented as an SKI, the SKI MUST equal the X.509 SKI extension in the trust anchor's certificate. The router SHOULD include the TA options in the advertisement for which the certification path was found.

As in RFC 3971, if the router cannot find a path to the requested anchor, it SHOULD send an advertisement without any certificate, and SHOULD include the TA options that were solicited.
sections.plainLanguage: The router checks that the fingerprint matches the real authority. If it cannot find the authority, it says so without sending any certificate.

sections.title: IANA and Security Considerations
sections.content:
IANA updated the "Trust Anchor option (Type 15) Name Type field" registry with the values above. The registration procedure changed from Standards Action to Standards Action or IESG Approval.

The hashes have reasonable random properties, giving reasonably unique identifiers. If two identical identifiers occur in the same validation path, the router stops fetching certificates after the first one. If that certificate was configured as a TA by a host, the router sends an incomplete list and SEND validation fails.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of numbers was updated. If two authorities ever got the same fingerprint, the check could fail, which is why the hashes need to be nearly unique.

items.desc: 160-bit SHA-1 hash of the subject public key.
